description: Replica Facebook account-deactivation page (the user has navigated through Settings → Your Facebook Information → Deactivation and Deletion → Continue to Account Deactivation). Deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates on a Social-media fixture where the dominant DP signature is RETENTION via personalized shaming + privacy preselects.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/fixtures/facebook-deactivation/facebook-deactivation.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type ∈ {settings, cancellation, account_management} AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'deactivate / leave Facebook'. Vague intents ('manage account', 'browse settings') or wrong ones ('post', 'find friends') are incorrect — the user came to leave, the page is trying to talk them out of it. Every downstream harm test depends on this being correctly identified as a leaving flow with deactivation intent.

dark_patterns.element: 'Daniel, Maya, and 4 other friends will miss you' banner with friend photo tiles + 'You'll be missed' tagline
dark_patterns.why: The shaming is in the LABEL/UI of the leaving action — Facebook personalizes the cost of leaving by surfacing specific named friends with their photos. The user can still proceed with deactivation, but the option is wrapped in emotional copy ('miss you', 'won't see your posts', 'won't know how to reach you') designed to make declining the deactivation feel like a betrayal of those specific people. Manipulation is in the framing, not the action. Iconic Facebook deactivation pattern documented in DP literature (Bösch 2016, Mathur 2019).

dark_patterns.element: Pre-selected 'Deactivate temporarily' radio with 'Recommended' pill tag — the option that auto-restores on next login
dark_patterns.why: The user navigated through 4 settings screens to GET to the deactivation page (high-intent signal that they want to leave). The pre-selection pushes the company-favoring option (temporary deactivation, which silently auto-restores on any login) over the option that matches the user's revealed intent (permanent deletion). Pre-selecting the company-favoring outcome inside a user-initiated leaving flow benefits Facebook (continued ad-revenue surface on accidental return) at the user's cost (silent reactivation of an account they thought was gone). Canonical Facebook pattern.

dark_patterns.element: 'Cancel Deactivation — Keep My Account' giant blue pill button (full-width, 16px bold, Facebook brand blue #1877f2) — vs the secondary 'Continue with Deactivation' bordered button below (CE-2)
dark_patterns.why: The user navigated through 4 settings screens to GET to the deactivation page. The visually dominant action in the action row is the CANCEL pill (full-width, bright Facebook blue #1877f2, 16px bold), while the option that matches the user's revealed intent (continue with deactivation — see CE-2) is a smaller secondary button. Prominence misaligned with revealed user intent — not a feature suggestion, a deliberate visual demotion of the user's chosen path.

counterexamples.element: 'Sign Out' link in the top nav header
counterexamples.why_not: A standard navigation link present on every Facebook page. Nothing on this deactivation page depends on the user signing out, and the link doesn't gate or coerce anything. Account-management nav affordances are routine.

counterexamples.element: The 'Continue with Deactivation' button — full-width, dark-bordered white button below the Cancel pill
counterexamples.why_not: This IS the legitimate deactivate CTA — does what its label promises (navigates to the deactivation-confirm step). Visually less prominent than the Cancel pill (DP-3) but NOT visually buried: full-width, clearly bordered, easily clickable, label exactly matches the action. The harm test for False hierarchy requires the legitimate option be visually buried (e.g., 9px gray no-underline link); this button doesn't meet that test. Compare DP-3 (the visually-dominant misaligned-with-intent CTA which IS the false-hierarchy DP).

counterexamples.element: Pre-checked 'Email me a confirmation when this completes' checkbox
counterexamples.why_not: A pre-checked checkbox inside a settings flow — visually adjacent to DP-2 (the pre-selected temp-deactivate radio) — but the option is a sensible transactional default: sending the user a record of an account-state change they just initiated. Not a paid add-on, not marketing, not data extraction. Compare DP-2 (Recommended-tagged pre-selected radio that pushes a Facebook-favoring option) — same surface shape, opposite harm-test answer.

counterexamples.element: 'Recently active friends' card listing actual friend names + last-active timestamps
counterexamples.why_not: Same friend-photo UI surface as DP-1 (the 'will miss you' shaming banner), but here the content is purely INFORMATIONAL — a friend list with real last-active timestamps that Facebook genuinely has. No 'will miss you' framing, no 'they need you', no shaming language; just an informational reminder of who the user knows on the platform. Informs rather than pressures. The DP-1 vs CE-4 contrast is the most useful test of the model's harm-test discrimination on this fixture: same UI primitive, opposite harm-test answer.

counterexamples.element: 'Need a hand? Visit our Help Center' link in the page footer
counterexamples.why_not: A footer help link is not coercive friction — it's an optional support affordance that the user can ignore entirely while completing deactivation. The harm test for Forced Action requires the user be FORCED to take an action; this link doesn't force anything.

fixture_notes: 3 DPs after the 2026-05 realism audit (issue #27). Originally 6 DPs; dropped 3 as not canonical for current Facebook deactivation UX: dp-fake-stats (Facebook does not surface a '98% reactivate' statistic on the deactivation page; their main retention is the friend-faces shaming, DP-1), dp-hidden-data-terms (Facebook actually surfaces deactivation behavior inline as part of the shame/retention copy — it is not hidden), dp-forced-reason (the reason picker is currently OPTIONAL in real Facebook UX, not a required gate — the 'must select' framing is a stretch).

The remaining 3 DPs are all canonical Facebook patterns: friend-photo personalized shaming (DP-1 — iconic, in DP literature), temp-deactivation preselect with auto-restore (DP-2 — canonical FB nudge), Cancel pill dominance vs Continue Deactivation (DP-3).

DP-1 (friend-faces shaming) and CE-4 (recent-friends informational list) remain the most useful contrast pair on this fixture — same friend-photo UI primitive, opposite harm-test answer. Pre-audit these were DP-1 and CE-4; post-audit the gt_ids are unchanged.
Disguised ad, Trick wording, Pop-up ad, Hidden information, Fake social proof, and Forced Action have no coverage on this fixture by design — see issue #27 for the cross-fixture rationale.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 3, the count of injected dark patterns post-audit]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags) — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets
Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is no longer bounded by the schema cap on this fixture.
